source.title: Towards Understanding Safety Alignment: A Mechanistic Perspective from Safety Neurons
source.authors: Jian-Hui Chen; Xiaozhi Wang; Zijun Yao; Yushi Bai; Lei Hou; Juan-Zi Li

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present, though some tables are flattened in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports causal tests of selected MLP-neuron activation patching, not of the residual-stream difference-in-means direction or any of the listed claim versions. Its safety-cost outcomes are relevant to safety-neuron mechanisms but do not measure refusal rates.
record.gate_note: The paper finds neurons by contrasting SFT and DPO MLP activations, then patches selected neurons dynamically. It does not test the claim's single residual-stream direction, project that direction out, add it, perform an abliteration weight edit, or measure refusal as a distinct behavior. Table 8's cost scores for safety-neuron patching are recorded as findings about a related safety mechanism, not as results for a claim version. General-capability benchmark results are described in Table 8 and as marginal degeneration, but concern this different neuron intervention.
record.test_reason: The study identifies MLP 'safety neurons' by contrasting SFT and DPO activations, then patches DPO activations into Base and SFT models. It scores safety with a cost model. It never computes, ablates or adds a harmful-minus-harmless residual-stream direction, makes no weight edit, and measures no refusal rate. Arditi et al. (2024) appears only as a related-work citation. Its results bear on no claim version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors find that ~5% of MLP neurons are sparse, causally effective and stable across seeds: patching them recovers over 90% of DPO safety, with negligible or marginal general-capability change. Safety and helpfulness neurons overlap but need different activation patterns, which they offer as an explanation of alignment tax. They also report that a safeguard classifier on these neurons' activations can predict unsafe outputs before generation.
record.recipe_differences: The paper contrasts SFT and DPO MLP-neuron activations and dynamically patches selected neuron activations during generation. It does not use the harmful-minus-harmless residual-stream mean direction, project a direction out, or add one.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that the prompt dataset used to identify neurons affects causal patching effectiveness; similar prompt types yield more similar effects, and safety neurons work best on safety-related prompts. It also reports some differences by model and neuron-finding choices such as compared models and token positions.

fits_no_version.finding: Patching the top ~5% of MLP neurons (ranked by SFT-vs-DPO change score) with DPO activations lowers cost scores toward DPO levels across four red-teaming benchmarks and four model families, far more than random neurons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety-aligned behaviour is causally mediated by a sparse set of MLP neurons whose activations DPO alters; this is a neuron-level result, not about a residual-stream refusal direction.

fits_no_version.finding: Safety and helpfulness neurons overlap strongly. Patching activations between safety-DPO and helpfulness-DPO models trades one objective for the other (Table 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Alignment tax arises from competing activation patterns on a shared set of neurons.

record.problems: The paper evaluates safety with a learned cost model, rather than a direct refusal-rate measure; GPT-4 is also reported in an appendix. The work uses (IA)3 fine-tuning and acknowledges that effects with full-parameter fine-tuning are unknown. Safety cost outcomes do not establish the claimed direction's causal role. Table 8 reports benchmark scores, while the stated general-capability effect is characterized as marginal degeneration.
record.rows_left_out: Table 8's general-capability benchmark scores for patched and unpatched checkpoints are not separately rowed: they are outcomes of the different neuron-patching intervention and do not test any listed direction claim version. Table 1's causal-effect and aggregate general-performance-change results are also not separately rowed; its flattened layout makes reliable model/checkpoint-to-value assignment unclear in the supplied text.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means residual direction, no directional ablation or addition, no refusal rate.
No weight-edit abliteration of released models.
No analysis of jailbreaks suppressing a direction; no adversarial training against ablation.
No comparison of single-direction, affine or cone structure.
No separation of harmfulness representation from the refusal decision.
No cross-language or base-to-instruct transfer of a refusal direction.
Uses SFT/DPO with (IA)3 but does not test whether training determines a removable refusal direction.

record.verdict_notes: The relation is changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only': the original refusal-direction paper is cited once, in related work, with no argument about it. In flattened Table 8, the fourth numeric column after each block is JL and the fifth is PPL. The reader misread that column in r4, r8, r20 and r28; the corrected values are above. All rows correctly carry versions ['none'].

versions.untested_parts: No harmful-minus-harmless residual-stream direction, all-layer/all-position ablation or addition, refusal-rate measurement, or claimed capability-preservation test for that direction.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration evaluation.
No test of whether attacks suppress the claimed direction, or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
No test distinguishing a single direction from an affine structure, cone, or dominant direction plus others.
No separate measurement of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
No test of transfer of the claimed direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
The paper uses SFT and DPO training but does not test whether training choices determine whether the claimed removable direction exists.

relation.reason: Arditi et al. 2024 appears once, in a related-work sentence grouping it under RepE (and loosely describing it as linking features to attention heads). There is no further discussion and no experiment on it.

tranche.reason: The study patches DPO MLP-neuron activations into Base/SFT models and scores safety with a cost model. It never computes, ablates or adds a difference-in-means residual direction and reports no refusal rate, so it neither tests nor uses the finding.

source_check.notes: Table 8 is flattened in the text (Llama2/Gemma/Qwen HB-JL listed as row pairs, Mistral as columns). Every checked cell matches Table 1's causal effects. r4 and r20 still hold PPL values and need the verdict fixes applied. The 'over 90%' headline holds mainly for SFT; Table 1 'Ours' causal effects for Base models are often 56-88% (e.g. Llama2 Base 56/65/63/78).
